title: Building the agent step by step
notes: Start with the smallest loop that runs, then add one tool or feature at a time.
After every change, run Scout on a real question and read the trace before moving on.
When something breaks, the cause is almost always the last piece you added.

slides.title: Building the agent step by step
slides.sub: Smallest loop first, then one piece at a time, running it after every change
sentences: You have a scope and a drawing.
Now you build Scout, and the order you build it in matters as much as the code.
This lesson shows one habit that keeps your agent working at every step.

slides.title: Two ways to build

left.label: All at once
points: Write six tools, memory and tests
Run everything for the first time
Twelve errors, no idea which change

right.label: One piece at a time
points: Start with a loop that runs
Add one tool, then run it
Each error points to one change
A working Scout at every step

sentences: Picture two ways to build Scout.
In the first, you write all six tools, the memory and the tests, then run it for the first time.
It fails in twelve places, and you can't tell which change caused which error.
Everything is new, so everything is a suspect.
In the second, you start with the smallest thing that runs, and add one piece at a time.
When something breaks, only one thing changed, so you know exactly where to look.
And you always have a Scout that works, even if it can't do much yet.

slides.title: The build loop

note.text: If the check fails, the bug is in the piece you just added.

sentences: The habit is a small loop of your own, and you go round it many times.
Build: add one small piece, like a single tool.
Run: ask Scout a real customer question that needs that piece.
Check: read the trace and the reply, and compare them with the data.
Keep: when it works, save your work and choose the next piece.
If the check fails, you know the bug is in the piece you just added.

slides.title: Piece one: the smallest loop that runs
slides.lead: No tools yet. Just the model, Scout's system prompt and one customer question.

rows.out: reads your API key from the environment

rows.code: next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")

aside.label: Run it
aside.text: Ask about ORB-10482. With no tools, Scout should say it can't look orders up yet. Honest is a pass.

sentences: The first piece is the smallest Scout that can run.
You create a client, which reads your API key from the environment.
You choose the model.
You call the messages create method with the model, the system prompt and the customer's question.
Then you take the text block out of the reply.
Run it with an order question: Scout should admit it can't look orders up yet, and that honesty is your first pass.

slides.title: Scout's build order

note.text: Every row ends with Scout running. Never two new pieces at once.

sentences: Here is the order we build Scout in.
First the bare loop, which should answer honestly that it can't look anything up.
Then the get order tool, checked by asking the same question and seeing one call with the right order number.
Then the track parcel tool, so the reply can say when the parcel will arrive.
Then the other four tools, each tested with its own question.
Finally memory and the trace, tested with a short two-turn chat.
Each row ends with Scout running, and you never add two new pieces at once.

slides.title: Adding one tool: get_order

note.text: Five small moves per tool. Only then the next one.

sentences: Adding one tool always takes the same five moves.
Define it: a name, a clear description and a schema for its input.
Write the function that does the work, here reading the order file.
Register it, both in the tools list the model sees and in the dispatcher that runs it.
Run Scout with a question that needs the new tool.
Read the trace: did Scout call the right tool with the right input?
Only when all five moves are done do you start on the next tool.

slides.title: Run, then check

messages.label: Scout
messages.text: Your Trailhead tent has shipped with ParcelPath. The tracking number is PP-88213.

messages.label: Your check
messages.text: Right tool, right input, and the facts match orders.json. Next piece: track_parcel.

aside.label: Notice
aside.text: No arrival day yet. That's expected: tracking is the next piece, not this one.

sentences: Here is the run right after adding the get order tool.
You ask the same question as before.
The trace shows one step: get order, with the right order number, returning shipped and a tracking number.
Scout's reply uses exactly those facts.
You compare them with the order file, they match, and this piece passes.
There's no arrival day yet, and that's expected: tracking is the next piece.

slides.title: When a step breaks
slides.scenario: Priya adds track_parcel and runs the same question again.

steps.text: Adds the track_parcel definition and its function
Runs it. The trace shows: Error: Unknown tool: track_parcel
Only one thing changed, so she checks the new tool's wiring
It was never added to run_tool. One line, run again: pass

result.text: Small steps turn a mystery into a three-minute fix.

sentences: Here is why the habit pays off.
Priya adds the track parcel tool: the definition and the function.
She runs the same question, and the trace shows an error: unknown tool.
Only one thing changed since the last good run, so she looks straight at the new tool's wiring.
She had forgotten to add it to the dispatcher. One line, run again, and it passes.
In an all-at-once build, that same error would hide among a dozen others.

slides.title: Recap

points.text: Start with the smallest loop that runs, even with no tools.
Add one piece at a time: define, write, register, run, check.
After every change, ask a real question and read the trace.
When it breaks, look first at the piece you just added.

sentences: Let's recap.
Start with the smallest loop that runs, even with no tools at all.
Add one piece at a time, using the same five moves for every tool.
After every change, run a real question and read the trace.
And when something breaks, the last piece you added is the first suspect.
Next, we look closely at the pieces themselves: Scout's six tools and its memory.

midQuiz.q: You added get_order and track_parcel together, and now Scout errors. What would the build loop have had you do?
options: Add them one at a time, running Scout after each
Write all six tools before running anything
Skip running until the test set is written
midQuiz.explain: With one change per run, an error points straight at its cause. Two changes at once means two suspects, and they can hide each other.
midQuiz.hint: How many things should change between two runs?

midQuiz.q: Your first Scout has no tools. Asked about an order, it says it can't look orders up yet. Is that a pass?
options: No: it should guess the most likely status
Yes: it runs, and it's honest about what it can't do
No: a loop with no tools is useless
midQuiz.explain: The first piece only has to run and behave honestly. Every later piece builds on a loop you already trust.
midQuiz.hint: What was the goal of the very first piece?

endQuiz.q: What are the five moves for adding one tool?
options: Write, deploy, wait for complaints, fix, repeat
Define, write, add to the prompt, test at the end, ship
Define, write, register, run a question, read the trace
endQuiz.explain: Each tool is defined, written, registered in TOOLS and the dispatcher, then run with a real question and checked in the trace before the next tool starts.
endQuiz.hint: The last move is where you check your work.

endQuiz.q: Right after adding a tool, the trace says Unknown tool: track_parcel. Where should Priya look first?
options: The model: it is inventing tool names
The wiring of the tool she just added, such as run_tool
endQuiz.explain: The model asked for a tool it was told about, but the dispatcher didn't know it. The error appeared right after one change, so that change is the first suspect.
endQuiz.hint: What changed since the last good run?
